Advanced photovoltaics, such as ultra-ﬂexible perovskite solar cells (UF-PSCs), which are known for their
lightweight design and high power-to-mass ratio, have been a long-standing goal that we, as humans, have
continuously pursued. Unlike normal PSCs fabricated on rigid substrates, producing high-efﬁciency UF-PSCs re-
mains a challenge due to the difﬁculty in achieving full coverage and minimizing defects of metal halide
perovskite (MHP) ﬁlms. In this study, we utilized Al2O3 nanoparticles (NPs) as an inorganic surface modiﬁer to
enhance the wettability and reduce the roughness of poly-bis(4-phenyl) (2,4,6-trimethylphenyl) amine simulta-
neously. This approach proves essentials in fabricating UF-PSCs, enabling the deposition of uniform and dense
MHP ﬁlms with full coverage and fewer defects. We systematically investigated the effect of Al2O3 NPs on ﬁlm
formation, combining simulation with experiments. Our strategy not only signiﬁcantly increases the power
conversion efﬁciency (PCE) from 11.96% to 16.33%, but also promotes reproducibility by effectively addressing
the short circuit issue commonly encountered in UF-PSCs. Additionally, our UF-PSCs demonstrates good me-
chanical stability, maintaining 98.6% and 79.0% of their initial PCEs after 10,000 bending cycles with radii of 1.0
and 0.5 mm, respectively.

high power-to-mass ratio, enabling many potential applications like

probes, weather balloons, high altitude airships, unmanned space sta-
tions, etc [1–4]. Metal halide perovskites (MHPs), which have been
widely known to the public thanks to their excellent photo-electronic

achieving controllable deposition of MHP ﬁlms and establishing strong
interfacial coupling on ultra-ﬂexible substrates [16–19].

conductive polymer poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sul-
fonate (PEDOT:PSS, PH 1000) is a popular choice as an electrode for
organic solar cells and PSCs due to its superior ﬁlm processability and
mechanical durability compared to the rigid and brittle ITO electrode. As
PEDOT:PSS (unless otherwise speciﬁed, PEDOT:PSS will refer to
PEDOT:PSS PH 1000) is a p-type organic semiconductor, UF-PSCs typi-
cally are in a p-i-n architecture of Ag/BCP/PCBM/MHP/PEDOT:PSS/PET
[9,15]. Modulation of the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS layer is essential in
the fabrication of high-efﬁciency devices. For example, Vaagensmith
et al. reported the use of additive and plasma treatment to decrease the
sheet resistance of PEDOT:PSS, which then served as a good transparent
electrode for ITO-free PSCs [25]. Hu and coworkers also demonstrated
the use of an ionic additive to improve conductivity, transmittance, and
mechanical endurance [26]. For UF-PSCs, it is not sufﬁcient to use
PEDOT:PSS alone to selectively extract photoinduced holes or block
photoinduced electrons. Therefore, to achieve high performance in
UF-PSCs, it is crucial to use appropriate hole transport materials (HTMs)
such as nickel oxide (NiOx) and poly-bis(4-phenyl) (2,4,6-trimethyl-
phenyl) amine (PTAA) [27–29]. PTAA is one of the most widely used
HTMs in inverted PSCs owing to a lower parasitic absorption and a better
energy band alignment with MHP [7,30,31]. Whereas, PTAA's high
surface energy and subsequent poor wettability may cause discontinuity
or pinholes in the MHP layer [32,33]. Conventional methods to improve
the wettability of MHP ﬁlms on hydrophobic substrates, such as pre-
washing with dimethylformamide (DMF), may be not sufﬁcient as it
usually results in incomplete ﬁlm coverage. To overcome these limita-
tions and achieve high-performance UF-PSCs, alternative methods must
be explored to ensure complete coverage and strong interfacial coupling
of MHP ﬁlms on PTAA for ultra-ﬂexible substrates.
Here, we report the utilization of Al2O3 nanoparticles (NPs) as an
inorganic surface modiﬁer to enhance the wettability and reduce the
roughness of PTAA simultaneously. This strategy enables good afﬁnity
between the substrate and MHP precursor solution, in turn attaining
uniform and dense MHP ﬁlms with full coverage and fewer defects,
which proves essential in fabricating UF-PSCs. Combined with computer
simulations, we systematically investigated the effect of Al2O3 NPs on
spin-coating and ﬁlm formation. This strategy not only signiﬁcantly in-
creases PCE from ~12% to over 16%, but also promotes reproducibility
by effectively addressing the short circuit issue commonly encountered in
the ﬁeld of UF-PSCs. Moreover, our UF-PSCs demonstrates good me-
chanical stability, maintaining 98.6% and 79.0% of their initial PCEs
after 10,000 bending cycles with radii of 1.0 and 0.5 mm, respectively.
2. Results and discussion
As illustrated in Fig. 1, we present the preparation process of UF-PSCs.
Firstly, Ultra-ﬂexible polyethylene terephthalate (UF-PET) was lami-
nated onto a smooth glass surface using Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) as
an adhesive layer. PEDOT:PSS was then spin-coated onto the PET. To
facilitate the extraction of photogenerated holes, a PTAA layer was spin-
coated onto PEDOT:PSS prior to the deposition of a MHP light-absorbing
layer. Precise control over the deposition of MHP ﬁlms and strong
interfacial coupling with PTAA on ﬂexible substrates is crucial for the
preparation of high performance UF-PSCs. [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid
methyl ester (PCBM) and bathocuproine (BCP) layers were sequentially
deposited by a spin-coating process. The integrated UF-PSCs device was
obtained after the deposition of the Ag electrode, which was ﬁnally
peeled off from the glass substrate. It is important to note that the surface
wettability and roughness of the substrate prior to MHP deposition are
crucial factors in the fabrication of high-efﬁciency UF-PSCs.
As a result of the strong hydrophobic nature of the PTAA surface,
achieving a uniformly coated MHP ﬁlm through direct spin-coating of the
MHP precursor onto the PTAA surface presents a challenge, as depicted
in Fig. 2a. To overcome the challenge of obtaining a uniformly coated
MHP ﬁlm on the hydrophobic PTAA surface, a DMF prewashing strategy
has been frequently employed. However, even after DMF prewashing, the
ﬁlm coverage remains inadequate, as shown in Fig. 2b. The limited af-
ﬁnity of DMF on PTAA restricts the enhancement of wettability, and the
prewashing process with DMF can compromise the glove box atmo-
sphere, negatively impacting subsequent deposition and crystallization
of MHP. To address this issue, a low-temperature processed layer of
Al2O3 NPs was deposited on PTAA. The abundant surface hydroxyl
groups endow Al2O3 NPs with excellent amphiphilic properties, allowing
them to bind not only to PTAA but also to the MHP solution. Conse-
quently, the modiﬁcation with Al2O3 signiﬁcantly enhances the wetta-
bility of the PTAA surface, enabling complete coverage of the substrate
by the MHP solution. This leads to the formation of a high-quality MHP
ﬁlm and ultimately a superior device, as illustrated in Fig. 2c. For sub-
sequent discussion, the PTAA without any treatment, with DMF pre-
washing, and with a covering of Al2O3 NPs are referred to as “control”,
“DMF PW”, and “Al2O3 SM”, respectively. We utilized Al2O3 NPs
dispersed in isopropyl alcohol (IPA) instead of an aqueous dispersion
system, since IPA is an organic solvent, which spreads well on hydro-
phobic PET surfaces. In Fig. S3, we provide photos demonstrating the
spreading of the Al2O3 IPA dispersion on the hydrophobic PET.

in terms of hole extraction, but its hydrophobic nature weakens the

Covering PTAA with Al2O3 NPs is a good strategy to address this issue,
which can signiﬁcantly reduce the contact angle from 31.1 to 14.7.
In addition to surface wettability, surface roughness is another crucial
factor that requires careful consideration. Unlike the rigid glass substrate,
commercially available ultra-thin ﬂexible PET substrates have a signiﬁ-
cantly large surface roughness. However, this can be reduced through the
sequential deposition of other layers such as PEDOT:PSS, PTAA, and
Al2O3 NPs by spin-coating (Fig. S4). The effect is particularly noticeable
when depositing an Al2O3 NPs layer, which can remarkably reduce the
surface roughness Sa from 723 nm to 348 nm. To ﬁgure out the distri-
bution of Al2O3 NPs on PTAA, the 3D-SLCM was employed to evaluate
the roughness of the PTAA/PEDOT:PSS/PET and generated a 3D
morphological proﬁle, as depicted in Fig. 3d and Fig. S5. Subsequently,
we simulated the distribution of Al2O3 NPs on PTAA by means of sim-
center STAR-CCM þ simulation, as illustrated in Fig. 3e. The Al2O3 NPs
can ﬂatten the rough surface of PTAA/PEDOT:PSS/PET by ﬁlling the
concave region, in turn resulting in a relatively smooth substrate, as
conﬁrmed by the SEM image in Fig. 3c. Meanwhile, we prepared four
samples: PET, PEDOT:PSS/PET, PTAA/PEDOT:PSS/PET, Al2O3/PTAA/
PEDOT:PSS/PET. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) images, illustrated in
Fig. S6, were then captured. The results obtained indicate a lack of cor-
respondence between the observed roughness and morphological
changes and the outcomes of our distribution simulation. The analysis of
the reasons is as follows: Unlike the morphology of conventional devices
(on rigid or normal ﬂexible substrate), the substrates of ultra-ﬂexible
substrate (~10 μm) often display a broad range of undulations. The
AFM characterization method is typically limited to observing micro-
scopic roughness and morphology due to its viewport range constraint.
The relatively more macroscopic undulations cannot be measured by
AFM characterization, resulting in disparities between the roughness
results output by AFM characterization and the simulation results. In our
simulation model, the substrate dimensions exceed 700 μm in length and
width, while the 3D-SLCM offers a viewport range of up to a millimeter.
Therefore, we consider the 3D-SLCM results to provide more compelling
evidence compared to the AFM results. Each image in Fig. S5 has a
viewport range of 1 mm  1 mm.
As aforementioned, the surface properties of these substrates differ
signiﬁcantly. To further analyze the effect of these differences on MHP
formation, we conducted ﬁnite element simulations of spin-coating MHP
precursor solutions on various substrates. The surface energy of each
substrate was obtained through contact angle measurements, while other
substrate parameters regarding surface roughness were determined using
3D-SLCM. The simulation results, which indicate the spreading speed of
the MHP precursor solution on the control and Al2O3 SM substrates, are
clearly presented in Fig. 3f and g. In our simulation, we deﬁne the length
of the viewport occupied by the original droplet as the normalized length
“1". At t¼1.5 s, 1.5 s after the start of spin-coating, the MHP precursor
solution on the control substrate spreads to L¼2.33. However, this then
surprisingly shrinks back to L¼1.83 at t¼2 s (as shown in Fig. 3f). The
difﬁculty in the MHP precursor solution spreading on PTAA is due to the
relatively larger interface energy between PTAA and MHP precursor
solution. It therefore becomes clear that achieving complete coverage of
the MHP precursor solution on an untreated PTAA surface is impossible.
In comparison to the untreated PTAA surface of the control substrate, the
Al2O3 SM substrate has lower interface energy with the MHP precursor
solution. As a result, the spreading speed of the MHP precursor solution
on the Al2O3 NPs-coated PTAA surface is much faster than that on un-
treated PTAA. For instance, by t¼1.5 s, the MHP precursor solution
spreads to L¼4.56 and continues spreading to nearly cover the entire
viewport by t¼2.0 s. It can be concluded that both the reduction in sur-
face roughness and the enhancement of surface wettability contributed to
the facilitated spreading of the MHP precursor solution.

other related mechanisms. Fig. 6c and Table S3 demonstrate that the

hysteresis of the Al2O3 SM-based devices is negligible. The presence of

peeling off the substrate during bending.
3. Conclusion
In summary, we conducted a comprehensive study on the preparation
of UF-PSCs, with a focus on utilizing Al2O3 as a surface modiﬁer to
address a common problem encountered in the ﬁeld of UF-PSCs. Our
investigation encompassed the mechanical properties, morphology, and
semiconductor optoelectronics of MHPs deposited on substrates with
different roughness and wettability. We highlighted the positive effects
of the Al2O3 NPs on improving the crystalline quality of MHP, the
reproductivity, and the PCE of UF-PSCs. By employing this approach, we
achieved a high PCE of 16.33% in UF-PSCs with excellent bending
tolerance. While further improvements in PCE and scalability of large-
area devices are necessary for practical applications, our work provides
valuable insights into the development of ﬂexible photovoltaics. We
believe that our ﬁndings will signiﬁcantly contribute to the advancement
of UF-PSCs research and inspire further exploration in this exciting ﬁeld.

each group utilizing distinct substrates. The statistical PCE values of these
devices are presented in Fig. 6b and Table S2. Furthermore, we have
included the J-V curves of the most superior device from each group,
showcasing both forward and backward scanning directions, in Fig. 6c.
When fabricating UF-PSCs on the control substrate, a signiﬁcant number
of devices, exceeding 50%, experience complete short circuits, leaving
only 10–20% of devices with mediocre performance. The highest-
performing device on the control substrate is only able to achieve a
modest PCE of 11.96%. Limited improvement can be observed in the case
of DMF PW-based UF-PSCs, but it is noteworthy that 40% of the devices
still suffer from short circuit issues. While the DMF prewashing treatment
has been utilized to enhance the PCE of rigid p-i-n PSCs, our ﬁndings
suggest that this method falls short in addressing the wetting issues that
arise in the realm of UF-PSCs. Two primary factors contribute to the low
yields and poor repeatability observed in both the control and DMF PW-
based devices. There are two primary factors that contribute to this
challenge. The ﬁrst factor is the presence of numerous pinholes and
cracks, leading to incomplete coverage of the MHP ﬁlms on PTAA. The
second factor is a high degree of surface roughness, which causes the
device electrodes to connect and results in short circuits. Thanks to the
full coverage of MHP ﬁlm, the Al2O3 SM-based devices exhibit excep-
tional reproducibility and do not experience any short circuit problems,
achieving 100% yields and high repeatability. Impressively, the Al2O3
SM-based devices achieve an average PCE of approximately 15%.
Moreover, the most outstanding UF-PSCs in our current investigation
exhibit a JSC of 24.59 mA cm/C02,aVOC of 1.046 V, and a ﬁll factor (FF) of
63.49%, ultimately achieving a remarkable PCE of 16.33%. This PCE is
higher than that of either the DMF PW-based (12.20%) or the control
(11.96%) devices. It is worth noting that the JSC value mentioned above
is consistent with the integrated photocurrent obtained from the external
quantum efﬁciency (EQE) measurement, as shown in Fig. S9.
The hysteresis phenomenon observed in both backward and forward
J-V scanning directions for PSCs has been extensively reported in pre-
vious literature. This phenomenon is associated with multiple factors,
including ion migration, defects, interfacial charge recombination, and
other related mechanisms. Fig. 6c and Table S3 demonstrate that the
degree of hysteresis varies signiﬁcantly among the three champion UF-
PSCs. In comparison to the control and DMF PW-based devices, the
hysteresis of the Al2O3 SM-based devices is negligible. The presence of
cracks and pinholes as well as high defect density in the active layer
(MHP) are major reasons responsible for the signiﬁcant hysteresis
observed in the case of the control or DMF PW-based device. By SCLC
characterization, we calculated that the defect density of states of Al2O3
SM devices is much lower compared to control devices, which is one of
the reasons for the reduced hysteresis. Furthermore, we tested the tran-
sient photovoltage (TPV) decay curves of the optimized ﬁlms and control
devices. As shown in Fig. S10, the Al2O3 SM-based device exhibits a
carrier recombination lifetime that is much higher than that of the con-
trol device. This is in good agreement with the enhanced integrity of the
MHP/PTAA interface and explains the low degree of hysteresis.
For Al2O3 SM devices that exhibit both a low FF, we provide the
following explanation: the FF of a device is primarily determined by the
series resistance, bypass resistance, and characteristics of the PN junc-
tion. An increase in series resistance, a decrease in bypass resistance, and
the presence of defects and impurities within the PN junction, and other
unfavorable conditions, contribute to a reduction in the FF. To achieve
ultra-ﬂexible bending, we utilize PEDOT:PSS as the electrode material,
which offers greater resistance to bending compared to ITO. However, it
should be noted that the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS is inferior to that of
ITO, resulting in a reduced FF for the device. To isolate the impact of
substrate conductivity on the reduced FF, we prepared devices with an
identical structure on ITO substrates. The J-V curves of the ITO device
and ultra-ﬂexible device are presented in Fig. S11. The results demon-
strate that ITO devices can attain a FF of 82% when the reduction in FF
caused by substrate conductivity is excluded.
To evaluate the mechanical durability of our UF-PSCs, we conducted
bending tolerance tests using a bending radius of 1.0 mm and 0.5 mm,
respectively. Following the scheduled bending cycles, we conducted J-V
tests to collect the PV parameters of the UF-PSCs. Fig. 6d and e depict the
normalized PCE of the UF-PSCs as a function of bending cycles. Our re-
sults demonstrate that the PCE of DMF PW-based UF-PSCs decreases to
47.6% (radius¼1 mm) and 58.9% (radius¼0.5 mm) of the initial PCE
after only 500 bending circles, while the control UF-PSCs can maintain
60.2% (radius¼1 mm) and 78.3% (radius¼0.5 mm) of the initial PCE
under the same conditions. This result suggests that the DMF PW-based
UF-PSCs exhibit inferior mechanical properties compared to the control
devices. This could be attributed to non-uniform stress release during
bending. Uneven stress release leads to a quicker fracturing of the ﬁlm,
resulting in a faster decline in PCE. In contrast, the Al2O3 SM-based de-
vices demonstrate impressive bending stability, maintaining 98.6%
(radius¼1 mm) and 79.0% (radius¼0.5 mm) of the initial PCE after
10,000 bends. We postulate that the enhanced contact between the MHP
and PTAA interfaces facilitated by the addition of Al2O3 NPs reinforces
the interfacial mechanical coupling, thereby shielding the ﬁlm from
peeling off the substrate during bending.
3. Conclusion
In summary, we conducted a comprehensive study on the preparation
of UF-PSCs, with a focus on utilizing Al2O3 as a surface modiﬁer to
address a common problem encountered in the ﬁeld of UF-PSCs. Our
investigation encompassed the mechanical properties, morphology, and
semiconductor optoelectronics of MHPs deposited on substrates with
different roughness and wettability. We highlighted the positive effects
of the Al2O3 NPs on improving the crystalline quality of MHP, the
reproductivity, and the PCE of UF-PSCs. By employing this approach, we
achieved a high PCE of 16.33% in UF-PSCs with excellent bending
tolerance. While further improvements in PCE and scalability of large-
area devices are necessary for practical applications, our work provides
valuable insights into the development of ﬂexible photovoltaics. We
believe that our ﬁndings will signiﬁcantly contribute to the advancement
of UF-PSCs research and inspire further exploration in this exciting ﬁeld.

perovskite precursor solution was spread on the Al2O3-coated substrate
